item.title: Why Back-to-School Is So Overwhelming for Parents With ADHD
item.description:
ADHD

Why Back-to-School Is So Overwhelming for Parents With ADHD

Strategies to help parents with ADHD make it through the start of the school year.

Posted September 30, 2026

Source: chipi1189 / Pexels

The first month of school is officially over. Are we tired yet?

September is often portrayed as a fresh start. New backpacks. New teachers. New routines.

But if you are a parent with ADHD, September can also feel like an organizational nightmare: Your inbox is filling up with messages from teachers. There are forms to complete, new online portals to figure out, extracurricular schedules to coordinate, lunches to make, and seemingly endless dates to remember. And if your child has ADHD or learning difficulties like you, you may also be trying to organize accommodations, communicate with resource teachers, and help a child who is struggling with their own transition back to school.

And all of this is happening while the rest of your life continues on as usual.

I often hear parents with ADHD describe feeling as though everyone else received an instruction manual that they somehow missed. Other parents seem to know when picture day is, remember to sign all the permission forms, and arrive at curriculum night on time. Meanwhile, you may find the email three days later while searching your inbox for something entirely unrelated. We often laugh at these experiences in retrospect but in the moment, they don't feel funny at all.

The Gap Between Planning and Doing

A friend of mine with ADHD, whom I'll call Chantal, once told me about missing her son's first parent-teacher meeting of the year.

The frustrating part was that Chantal had actually done almost everything right: She found the teacher's message in her crowded inbox, dealt with the new scheduling system, and chose an appointment time that worked with her work schedule. But she became distracted before adding the meeting to her calendar.

A week later, an email arrived from the teacher telling her what she missed at the meeting. Chantal was mortified. She followed her first instinct, which was not to reply. Embarrassment stopped her in her tracks, and Chantal closed her laptop. As the days passed, responding became increasingly uncomfortable. Eventually, that one missed meeting became part of a larger pattern of reduced communication with the school.

Chantal's experience captures something important about parenting with ADHD: She didn't miss the meeting because she wasn't interested in her son's education. In fact, she had put considerable effort into arranging it. The breakdown occurred in one tiny, but crucial, step between making the plan and remembering to carry it out. School asks parents to perform these small executive-function tasks over and over again: Read this. Remember that. Sign this. Bring that tomorrow. For an ADHD brain, the accumulation can become exhausting.

Source: Mikhail Nilov / Pexels

Don't Let One Dropped Ball Become 10

Many adults with ADHD have had years of experiences that left them sensitive to feeling as though they have disappointed someone. When a school mistake happens, it can be tempting to avoid it. We tell ourselves we'll answer the email later, once we have time to compose the perfect response. Then we forget again. By the time we remember, the embarrassment has grown.

If this happens to you this season, face the discomfort and try to interrupt the cycle early. You do not need a beautifully worded explanation; a brief response that acknowledges what happened and reconnects with the teacher is enough. The more realistic goal is to create systems that make remembering easier, and to repair quickly when those systems fail.

Build the Relationship Before There Is a Problem

One of the simplest things you can do at the beginning of the school year is introduce yourself to your child's teacher. Don't wait until your child is struggling; send a short email. Tell the teacher something your child is enjoying about the class. Let them know that you are interested in working together and that they can contact you if concerns arise. If you are comfortable disclosing that you have ADHD yourself, you might also explain that you sometimes benefit from clear reminders or direct communication.

This doesn't require a long email. The point is simply to make a connection. Later, if your child begins struggling, or you forget something, you are communicating with a person with whom you have already established some goodwill rather than introducing yourself in the middle of a problem. Early, positive contact can help establish a more collaborative relationship before difficulties arise.

Make Important Information Harder to Lose

Externalize as much information as you can. If your phone calendar works for you, use it consistently. Put school events into it as soon as you encounter them rather than assuming you'll remember later. Set reminders. If another system works better—a paper calendar on the refrigerator, alarms, sticky notes—use that instead.

The important part is not which organizational system you choose; it's reducing how much your brain is being asked to hold at once. External supports such as calendars, alarms, and reminders can make follow-through more manageable when consistency is required.

And be wary of adding more systems simply because September made you feel disorganized. Sometimes another app is not the answer. Chantal had successfully navigated the scheduling app; the problem was that the appointment never made it into the system she actually relied on. Use the tools that already work for your brain.

Give Yourself Some Wiggle Room

Back-to-school season places an extraordinary number of organizational demands on parents in a very short period of time. If you have ADHD, many of those demands fall directly in areas that are already difficult: keeping track of information, planning ahead, switching between tasks, remembering future obligations, and regulating emotions when something goes wrong.

So if it’s October and you already feel behind, resist turning that feeling into a judgment about your parenting.

Your child does not need you to execute the school year perfectly. They need you to remain engaged, to keep coming back when something falls through the cracks, and to maintain a workable relationship with the people who spend their days teaching them.

Somewhere this year, there will probably be a forgotten email, a missing form, or a morning when everyone leaves the house late. Deal with it. Repair it. Put the next important date in your calendar. And then move on with your day.

item.title: Underexplored Family Relationships: Twins
item.description:
Understanding Twins

Underexplored Family Relationships: Twins

Competition, comparison, and identity development related to twins.

Posted September 29, 2026

In my early life, twinship was usually seen as a very close relationship—and stressful for the family because of the extra work and energy required. Issues related to emotional and cognitive development were not seen as unusual or in need of special attention. The exception was the concern about “twin language.” How twins affected other siblings in their family was not considered deeply, if at all.

The closeness of twinship is a difficult identity problem that needs to be understood and addressed in a systematic way. The core issue is the separation anxiety that twins have when they are not with their twin. An example is young twins who are separated when they fight over a new toy that one of them received. For as long as they are apart, the twins will cry. The caregiver is at their wit’s end until the fight can be resolved and the twins can be reunited.

As my twin sister and I became older, twin development was studied at greater length, which fortunately uncovered the most effective way to raise twins and why. Individual development was stressed. Authentic relationships between family members and each twin that were personal and not concerned with “how the twins were alike” were essential.

Twins got a lot of attention for their look-alikeness, which was damaging if overdone. Our older brother had a sign in our double stroller that said, “Yes, they are twins,” because he was always asked this question. Parents today are more direct with the curiosity of onlookers, which they probably try to avoid.

Interest in twin development when I was young was very limited; my mother said that the only advice that she ever received was from a hospital nurse who told her to keep us separated. This input was helpful but very difficult to follow, as infants, babies, toddlers, and young twins want to be side by side like they were in the womb. Additionally, my mother needed more help figuring out how to handle her two troublemakers. When we were three years old, we explored the kitchen cupboards and drank red furniture polish because we thought it was yummy punch. Thankfully, our adventure was quickly discovered and the ambulance took us to the hospital where the doctor pumped our stomachs. My twin sister and I loved to tell this story.

A significant amount of time has passed since our family’s initial struggle with senseless questions that created problems for our brother. It is known that brothers and sisters are affected by the lives of the twins in the family. It is known that it is dangerous to let twins, or their siblings, decide how to take care of things. No longer do professionals suggest that Mom can do it on her own. How to parent twins is taken very seriously.

Competition and Comparison, and the Strong Need to Be Either Alike or Different

For better or worse, questions about which twin is the best and who has the most are very much a part of being a twin. The insistence on getting as much as your twin led my brother to measure, on a scale, how much food we were receiving. Who had more was a life and death issue. This “equality insanity” happens all of the time when parents do not know how to deal with competition and comparison, which can lead to fighting and unhappiness for all.

This Is Mine, and That Is Yours

From my own experiences, I've learned that twins, their siblings, and parents can have difficulties adjusting to one another as they grow up and develop. The “property management” issue is probably the most difficult twin problem for families to resolve. The intensity seen when one twin gets one less toy or cookie from Mom is amazing. I am still shocked at the determination that twins of all ages feel about everything being distributed equally.

I Want What You Have

This issue can be truly infuriating and last a very long time. Well into adulthood, many twins want the house, car, or vacation that their sister or brother has. Twins who are too close to one another have great difficulty “missing out” on what their twin has. More fortunate twins understand that they are different people and what they need may be different from their twin, which avoids fighting, unhappiness and possessiveness.

Conclusions

Sisters and brothers are at first confused by young twins entering the family because they fight and are jealous. At the same time, they have a hard time being separated and cry outrageously for their twin to be nearby. In addition, twins take whatever they want from their non-twin sister or brother without remorse. Understanding that their brother or sister is not the same as themselves is impossible to teach at an early age. Teaching twins that they need to wait takes a long time.

Twins get an enormous amount of attention, which can diminish their non-twin sibling’s sense of self-worth. On the other hand, anger and resentment toward each other are common, and twins often wish they were not twins because of the competition and comparison that goes on. Actually being asked about your twin is undermining to hear. I used to think, “Why are you not interested in what I am doing?”

Avoiding the “Look-A-Like Trap”

In my opinion, trying very hard to be yourself and present yourself as an individual will help you get along with all of your sisters and brothers better. Not seeing yourself as half of a whole is helpful for making new relationships with non-twins. Meeting new people without your twin sometimes eliminates the “Which one are you?” question that is seriously humiliating, no matter what your age.

What Parents Can Do to Decrease Questions About Their Twins

1. Dress your twin children in different outfits.

2. See each child as a unique individual by pointing out everyday things that they like and dislike.

3. Have special times you spend with each child doing different activities.

4. Find a parenting group on twins that you can attend on a regular basis.

5. Avoid labelling your twins as opposites of one another.

6. Do not show favoritism.

7. Talk with your family about how being a twin is different than being a single child.
